segments.text: From BBC Learning English.
This is Learning English from the News, our podcast about the news headlines.
In this programme: Trust in the news is the lowest it's ever been.
Hello, I'm Neil.
And I'm Georgie.
In this programme, we look at one big news story and the vocabulary in the headlines that will help you understand it.
You can find all the vocabulary and headlines from this episode, as well as a worksheet on our website, bbclearningenglish.com Let's hear more about this story.
Trust in news around the world is the lowest it has been since annual reports began in 2015.
The 2026 Digital News Report, published by the Reuters Institute, studied 48 markets, made up of countries and territories, and looked at the habits and attitudes surrounding online news consumption.
The report suggests that public trust in the news is at 27%, three points down from last year.
In the UK, trust is 20 points lower than it was ten years ago.
For the first time, social media and video networks are, on average, more popular than both TV and news websites and apps as sources of news.
The use of AI chatbots for news is also growing quickly.
Let's have our first headline.
This one is from BBC News.
Trust in news hits a new low, research suggests.
Again that headline from BBC News: Trust in news hits OK, so we've mentioned that trust in the news is lower than it has been since reports began.
And we're looking at this phrase 'a new low'.
Neil, is it connected?
Yes. A new low means the lowest level so far.
It's broken the previous record.
Here in the headline, the authors have used the verb 'hit'.
Trust in news hits a new low.
But it's also common to hear reach a new low or fall to a new low.
It can be used in many different contexts.
For example, the value of a country's currency has reached a new low, or the football players confidence hit a new low after he missed another penalty shot.
You're also likely to hear the opposite - a new high.
For example, house prices have hit a new high this month.
They're higher than they've ever been.
We've had a new low - The lowest level something has ever been.
For example, temperatures overnight fell to a new low.
This is Learning English from the News, our podcast about the news headlines.
Today we're talking about falling trust in news.
The use of traditional news sources like TV news and news websites is declining.
While social media and video networks are, for the first time, the most widely used way of accessing news.
Despite the increase in the use of social media and video networks for news, they are trusted less than traditional news media.
As the use of social media platforms for news increases, so do worries about misinformation or fake news.
But many people like the convenience of accessing news via social media.
Let's have our next headline.
This one from Press Gazette, a news organisation based in the UK: Publishing trends for 2026: Tech platforms overtake publishers as global news source.
And that headline again: Publishing trends for 2026: Tech platforms overtake publishers as global news source.
And that is from Press Gazette.
This headline is about the rise in the use of tech platforms as a news source.
Let's look at this word 'overtake' Georgie, what does it mean?
Well, let's think about the literal meaning of overtake first.
So imagine you're driving on a motorway and the car in front of you is going more slowly than you.
If you want to go faster, you need to overtake the car - to pass the car and go in front of it.
Right. And it's the same when I'm walking on a path and I want to move past the person in front of me who's going more slowly.
I can overtake that person.
Exactly.
Now, in the headline, it says tech platforms overtake publishers as global news source.
This is metaphorical, but it has the same idea.
It means tech platforms have moved ahead of traditional news sources which were previously in front.
Now, in other senses, overtake follows the same pattern as take.
It's an irregular verb, so overtook is the past and overtaken is the past participle.
Let's have another example.
Online sales have overtaken high street sales.
We've had overtake - move ahead of someone or something that was previously in front.
For example, I used to be better than Georgie at Spanish, but now, because she studies so hard, she's overtaken me.
She's much better than me now.
This is Learning English from the News from BBC Learning English.
We're talking about global trust in news sources.
The authors of the research note that while the 2025 report was relatively stable, in 2026, there are many changes which they say indicates a higher sense of uncertainty.
This year, there is a background of what they say is disruptive political, economic and social change.
And it is an unstable time for both the news sector and the world.
Let's have our next headline.
This one is from Global Investigative Journalism Network.
'Unsettled Time': 2026 Reuters Institute Digital Report finds rise of social media, video creators and AI chatbots amid falling news interest and audience trust.
That headline again from Global Investigative Journalism Network: 'Unsettled Time': 2026 Reuters Institute Digital Report finds rise of social media, video creators and AI chatbots
amid falling news interest and audience trust.
This time Neil, let's look at this word 'unsettled'.
The authors of the report say that we are in an unsettled time.
Yes. Let's look at the different parts of this word.
The verb settle can mean to live somewhere permanently.
So if you are settled, you are staying in one place.
OK, so if someone or something is unsettled, they are not staying the same.
Unsettled has a similar meaning to unstable or uncertain.
The authors say we are in an unsettled time because of political, economic and social change.
So unsettled can describe situations like in the headline- an unsettled time.
But unsettled is also an emotion.
Yes, it means your emotions are not stable, so you're a bit nervous and you don't feel calm at all.
For example, she felt unsettled after hearing the bad news, or the kids felt unsettled for a while after the family moved to a different country.
Compare unsettled with the word unsettling, which describes something that causes you to feel unsettled.
For example, watching the horror film on my own was quite unsettling.
I can imagine.
We've had unsettled - describes a situation or emotion that is not stable.
For example, the country headed into an unsettled time after the leader was removed.
That's it for this episode of Learning English from the News.
We'll be back next week with another news story.
And if you like learning English from the news and current affairs, follow the notes for this programme to find lots more.
There will be plenty to interest you.
Goodbye for now. Goodbye.
